title: Understanding Essay Writing: Structure and Argument
subject: LITERACY

authority.note: Grade 7 native candidate (Curriculum V2 draft). Not bound to an MOE objective or release, not reviewed, not approved, not published.

objectives.statement: Identify and explain the parts of an argumentative essay: an introduction that ends with a thesis statement, body paragraphs that each begin with a topic sentence, and a conclusion.
Build an argument by writing an arguable thesis statement with reasons and answering a counterargument.
Choose true, relevant and specific evidence for a reason and explain how it supports the claim in a PEEL paragraph.

scenes.title: Why write an argument?

content.body:
At a PTA meeting, parents and teachers disagree: should the school use its empty land for a **school garden**? Some people speak well, but a week later nobody remembers exactly what they said.

A written argument lasts. An **argumentative essay** puts your claim, your reasons and your evidence in an order a reader can follow, so they can judge your argument and maybe agree with you. Today you will learn that order and use it.

accessibility.textAlternative: Introduction: a PTA meeting disagrees about a school garden. A written argumentative essay organizes a claim, reasons and evidence so a reader can follow and judge it.

offline.fallback: Text, steps and questions are part of the saved lesson.

scenes.title: Warm-up: paragraphs and facts

content.body: Essays are built from paragraphs. Check what you remember. These answers are not marked.

items.prompt: What does a topic sentence do?
options: It tells the main idea of the paragraph
It gives the last small detail
It always asks the reader a question

feedback.correct: Yes. The topic sentence tells the reader what the whole paragraph is about, usually at the start.
feedback.incorrect: Details support the main idea. The topic sentence states the main idea itself, usually first.

optionFeedback: Yes. The topic sentence tells the reader what the whole paragraph is about, usually at the start.
Details support the main idea. The topic sentence states the main idea itself, usually first.
A question can be a hook, but a topic sentence states the paragraph's main idea.

items.prompt: Which sentence is a fact, not an opinion?
options: School gardens are the best thing a school can have.
Cassava leaves are grown and eaten in many parts of Liberia.
Everyone loves working in the garden.

feedback.correct: Yes. This can be checked, so it is a fact.
feedback.incorrect: 'The best' is a judgement, so this is an opinion. People could disagree.

optionFeedback: 'The best' is a judgement, so this is an opinion. People could disagree.
Yes. This can be checked, so it is a fact.
This is an opinion about how people feel, and it is not true of everyone.

accessibility.textAlternative: Two warm-up questions: what a topic sentence does, and which sentence is a fact. Each answer shows written feedback.

scenes.title: The three parts of an argumentative essay

content.body:
An argumentative essay has three parts, and each part has a job.

The **introduction** catches the reader's attention with a hook, gives a little background, and ends with the **thesis statement**: your claim and the main reasons for it.

Each **body paragraph** argues one reason. It starts with a **topic sentence**, then gives evidence and explains it. A strong essay also uses one paragraph to answer the other side.

The **conclusion** restates the thesis in new words, sums up the reasons, and ends with a final thought or a call to action. It does not add new reasons.
keyPoints: Introduction: hook, background, thesis statement.
Body: one reason per paragraph, each with a topic sentence, evidence and explanation.
Conclusion: restate, sum up, final thought. No new reasons.

accessibility.textAlternative: The three parts of an argumentative essay and the job of each: introduction with thesis, body paragraphs with topic sentences and evidence, and a conclusion that adds no new reasons.

media.alt: Essay structure: introduction with hook, background and thesis; body paragraphs, each with a topic sentence, evidence and explanation, one answering the other side; conclusion that restates, sums up and ends with a final thought.

scenes.title: Take apart a model essay plan

content.body: Here is a plan for the essay **Every school in Liberia should have a school garden**. Open each part to see what the writer put there and why.

steps.label: Introduction: hook
steps.description: Imagine eating fresh greens at lunch that you and your classmates grew yourselves. (A picture the reader can imagine pulls them in.)

steps.label: Introduction: thesis statement
steps.description: Every school in Liberia should have a school garden because gardens teach useful farming and science skills and give schools fresh food for learners. (Claim + two reasons.)

steps.label: Body paragraph 1: first reason
steps.description: Topic sentence: A school garden turns science and agriculture lessons into real work. The paragraph then gives evidence and explains it.

steps.label: Body paragraph 2: second reason
steps.description: Topic sentence: A garden can add fresh vegetables to school meals. Evidence and explanation follow.

steps.label: Body paragraph 3: the other side
steps.description: Some people say gardens take time away from lessons. But garden work can be part of science and agriculture lessons, done in short weekly sessions. (Objection, then answer.)

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.description: School gardens build skills and feed learners. Every school with land should start one this year. (Restate, sum up, call to action; no new reasons.)

accessibility.textAlternative: Six text steps of a model plan for 'Every school in Liberia should have a school garden': hook, thesis, two reason paragraphs, an answer to the other side, and a conclusion.

offline.fallback: Text, steps and questions are part of the saved lesson.

scenes.title: Guided practice: what makes a strong thesis

content.body:
A strong thesis statement is a **claim**: a sentence a sensible person could disagree with. It is specific, and it names the reasons the essay will argue.

A topic ('school gardens'), a plain fact ('some schools have gardens') or an announcement ('I will write about gardens') is not a thesis, because there is nothing to argue.
keyPoints: Claim: could someone disagree?
Specific: says exactly what should happen.
Reasons: names why, so the reader knows what is coming.

items.prompt: Which is the strongest thesis statement?
options: School gardens.
Some schools in Liberia have gardens.
Every school in Liberia should have a school garden because gardens teach farming skills and provide fresh food.
I will write about gardens in this essay.

feedback.correct: Yes. It is a claim someone could disagree with, it is specific, and it names two reasons.
feedback.incorrect: This is only a topic. It does not say what you think about gardens.

optionFeedback: This is only a topic. It does not say what you think about gardens.
This is a fact. Nobody would argue about it, so there is nothing to prove.
Yes. It is a claim someone could disagree with, it is specific, and it names two reasons.
This announces the topic but makes no claim.

items.prompt: Which sentence could a sensible person disagree with?
options: Monrovia is the capital of Liberia.
Students should have 30 minutes of reading time every school day because it builds vocabulary and confidence.
Many students go to school.

feedback.correct: Yes. Some people might say the time is needed for other subjects, so this claim can be argued.
feedback.incorrect: This is a fact that can be checked. It cannot be argued.

optionFeedback: This is a fact that can be checked. It cannot be argued.
Yes. Some people might say the time is needed for other subjects, so this claim can be argued.
This is a general fact, not a claim to argue.

accessibility.textAlternative: What makes a strong thesis, then two questions: choose the strongest thesis and choose the sentence someone could disagree with, each with written feedback.

scenes.title: Build a body paragraph with PEEL

content.body: A strong body paragraph follows **PEEL**: **P**oint, **E**vidence, **E**xplain, **L**ink. Open each step to build the first body paragraph of the garden essay.
keyPoints: The Explain sentence does not repeat the evidence. It says what the evidence shows and why that proves the point: 'This shows that…'.

steps.label: P: Point (topic sentence)
steps.description: A school garden turns science and agriculture lessons into real work.

steps.label: E: Evidence
steps.description: For example, in Musu's school garden, learners measure the beds, test which soil holds water best and record how fast each plant grows.

steps.label: E: Explain
steps.description: This shows that the garden makes learners practise measuring, testing and recording: skills they need in science class and on a family farm.

steps.label: L: Link
steps.description: So a garden makes lessons more useful, which is one reason every school should have one.

accessibility.textAlternative: A model PEEL paragraph in four text steps: point, evidence, explanation and link, about how a garden turns lessons into real work.

offline.fallback: Text, steps and questions are part of the saved lesson.

media.alt: PEEL paragraph: Point (a garden turns lessons into real work), Evidence (learners measure beds, test soil, record growth), Explain (they practise science and farming skills), Link (so every school should have a garden).

scenes.title: Choosing strong evidence

content.body:
Evidence is what makes a reader believe your reason. Four kinds are useful in school essays: **facts and figures** from a source you can name, **examples** of real events, the words of an **expert** (such as a teacher, nurse or agriculture officer), and your own **experience**.

Before you use evidence, test it with four questions. Never make up a fact or a number: if you use a figure, say where it comes from.

In this lesson, examples about **Musu's school** are made-up practice examples. They show what good evidence looks like, but they are not facts. In your own writing, use only evidence that is real.
keyPoints: Is it true, and can the reader check it?
Is it relevant: does it prove this reason?
Is it specific: who, what, where, when?
Where does it come from?

accessibility.textAlternative: Four kinds of evidence and four test questions for evidence, listed in the text and key points.

media.alt: Four kinds of evidence (facts and figures with a source, examples, expert words, experience) and four tests: is it true, is it relevant, is it specific, where does it come from.

scenes.title: Watch out: weak evidence and weak reasons

content.body: Writers often fall into these traps. Choose an answer for each question, then read the explanation.

items.prompt: Reason: a garden can add fresh vegetables to school meals. Which evidence supports this reason best? (Musu's school is the made-up practice school from this lesson.)
options: Gardens look beautiful when the flowers bloom.
At Musu's school, the agriculture club's greens and pepper were used in school lunches for a week last term.
Gardens are good, and everyone knows it.
Many countries have gardens.

feedback.correct: Yes. It is specific and it proves this exact reason: the garden added vegetables to school meals. In your own essay, use a real example like this from your school or community.
feedback.incorrect: This may be true, but it is about beauty, not school meals. It does not prove this reason.

optionFeedback: This may be true, but it is about beauty, not school meals. It does not prove this reason.
Yes. It is specific and it proves this exact reason: the garden added vegetables to school meals. In your own essay, use a real example like this from your school or community.
This is an opinion repeated, not evidence. The reader cannot check it.
This is too vague and says nothing about school meals.

items.prompt: Musa writes: 'School gardens are good because they are good for schools.' What is the problem?
options: Nothing. It is a strong argument.
It repeats the claim instead of giving a real reason.
The sentence is too long.

feedback.correct: Yes. A reason answers 'why?' with new information, such as 'because gardens give schools fresh food'.
feedback.incorrect: Look again: the reason only repeats the claim. It never says what the garden does.

optionFeedback: Look again: the reason only repeats the claim. It never says what the garden does.
Yes. A reason answers 'why?' with new information, such as 'because gardens give schools fresh food'.
Length is not the problem. The reason says nothing new.

items.prompt: Why should an argumentative essay mention the other side?
options: To show the writer has changed their mind.
To answer a likely objection, which makes the argument stronger.
To make the essay longer.

feedback.correct: Yes. Answering the strongest objection shows you have thought it through.
feedback.incorrect: The writer keeps their claim. They mention the other side in order to answer it.

optionFeedback: The writer keeps their claim. They mention the other side in order to answer it.
Yes. Answering the strongest objection shows you have thought it through.
Length is not the goal. Answering an objection makes the argument harder to reject.

accessibility.textAlternative: Three questions: choose the evidence that best supports a reason, spot a reason that repeats the claim, and explain why essays answer the other side.

scenes.title: Put a paragraph in PEEL order

content.body: These four sentences make one body paragraph, but they are mixed up. Put them in PEEL order: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link.
keyPoints: A. So when learners grow food at school, everyone eats better, which is why every school needs a garden.
B. Fresh vegetables from a school garden can make school meals healthier.
C. This shows that the garden gives the kitchen food it would otherwise have to buy or go without.
D. For example, at Musu's school the garden's greens and pepper were used in lunch for a whole week last term.

prompts.prompt: Write the four letters in PEEL order (for example: X, X, X, X), then say which letter is the topic sentence.

accessibility.textAlternative: Four mixed sentences labelled A to D, listed in the text. Type their letters in PEEL order.

offline.fallback: Write the four letters in PEEL order (for example: X, X, X, X), then say which letter is the topic sentence.

scenes.title: Plan before you write

content.body: Good writers plan first. Choose one topic and decide what you think. Then **brainstorm**: for two minutes, list every reason you can think of without judging them. Next, choose your **two strongest** reasons. For each one, write one piece of **real** evidence and where it comes from: something you saw, a fact you can check, or the words of someone you can name. If you cannot find real evidence for a reason, choose a different reason.
keyPoints: Topic 1: Every community should have a public library.
Topic 2: Schools should start each day with 20 minutes of reading.
Topic 3: Learners should help keep their school compound clean every week.
Plan: claim → reason 1 + evidence → reason 2 + evidence.

prompts.prompt: Brainstorm: list at least four reasons for your claim, one per line.
Your plan: write your claim, then your two strongest reasons, each with one piece of real evidence and where it comes from.

accessibility.textAlternative: Choose one of three topics, brainstorm at least four reasons, then write a plan: a claim and two reasons, each with real evidence and its source. Two text boxes.

offline.fallback: The plan is kept on the device until it can be sent.

scenes.title: Write your own thesis and PEEL paragraph

content.body: Now write, using your plan. Use only real evidence: an example you know, a fact you can check, or your own experience. Do not borrow Musu's school examples: they are made up. Your teacher reads this writing; it is not marked by this lesson.
keyPoints: Point: your first reason, as a topic sentence.
Evidence: one real, specific example or fact from your plan.
Explain: how the evidence proves the point.
Link: back to your claim.

prompts.prompt: Write the thesis statement from your plan: your claim and two reasons.
Write one body paragraph for your first reason using PEEL: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link.

accessibility.textAlternative: Using the plan from the previous scene, write a thesis statement and one PEEL body paragraph in two text boxes.

offline.fallback: Writing is kept on the device until it can be sent to the teacher.

scenes.title: Write a conclusion

content.body: Go back to the model plan for **Every school in Liberia should have a school garden**. Its body paragraphs argued two reasons (gardens teach farming and science skills, and they add fresh food to school meals) and answered one objection (garden work takes time from lessons). Write a conclusion of three or four sentences that does the three jobs of a conclusion. Do not copy the model plan's conclusion, and do not add a new reason.
keyPoints: Restate the thesis in new words.
Sum up the two reasons (and, if you like, the answer to the other side).
End with a final thought or a call to action.
Check: no new reasons.

prompts.prompt: Write your conclusion for the school-garden essay (three or four sentences).

accessibility.textAlternative: Write a three- or four-sentence conclusion for the school-garden essay: restate the thesis in new words, sum up its two reasons, end with a final thought, and add no new reason.

scenes.title: Peer review: one strength, one next step

content.body: Swap your PEEL paragraph with a partner and read it twice. Check it against the four questions below, then give honest, kind feedback: one **strength** and one **next step**. Talk about the writing, not the writer. If you are working alone, review your own paragraph the same way.
keyPoints: Point: does the topic sentence state a clear reason that matches the thesis?
Evidence: is it real and specific, and is its source named?
Explain: does a sentence show how the evidence proves the point?
Link: does the last sentence connect back to the claim?
Sentence starters: 'One strength is … because …' and 'Next time, try …'

prompts.prompt: Write one strength of the paragraph you reviewed. Name the question it meets and quote the words that show it.
Write one next step: name a question the paragraph does not yet meet and suggest one change.

accessibility.textAlternative: Swap PEEL paragraphs with a partner (or review your own), check the paragraph against four questions on point, evidence, explanation and link, then write one strength and one next step.

scenes.title: Write it again, on your own

content.body: Now show that you can do it alone. Use the second topic from your plan (or a new question you care about). Do not look back at the model plan or the hints. Use only real evidence and say where it comes from. Your teacher reads this writing; it is practice, not a mark.

prompts.prompt: Write a thesis statement for your second topic: your claim and two reasons.
Write one PEEL body paragraph that argues your first reason.
List the job of each sentence in your paragraph, in order (for example: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link).

scenes.title: Optional challenge: a full argumentative essay

content.body:
This challenge is optional. Try it if you finish early or want to go further; it is not part of the exit ticket.

Write a full essay on a question you care about, in five paragraphs: an introduction that ends with your thesis, two body paragraphs (one for each reason), one paragraph that answers the other side, and a conclusion that adds no new reason. Then write two sentences explaining which of your reasons is strongest and why.
keyPoints: Plan first: claim, two reasons, real evidence for each, and the strongest objection.
Answering the other side makes your argument stronger, not weaker.

accessibility.textAlternative: Optional challenge: write a five-paragraph argumentative essay on a question you care about, then explain which reason is strongest.

scenes.title: Key ideas to remember

content.body: Before the exit ticket, review the big ideas of this lesson.
keyPoints: An essay has an introduction (ending with the thesis), body paragraphs and a conclusion.
A thesis is a claim someone could disagree with, plus the reasons you will argue.
Each body paragraph follows PEEL: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link.
Strong evidence is true, relevant and specific, and you can say where it comes from.
Plan before you write: claim, two reasons, and real evidence for each.
Answer the other side; do not add new reasons in the conclusion.

accessibility.textAlternative: Review of five key ideas: essay parts, thesis, PEEL paragraphs, strong evidence, and answering the other side.
